Choose the reporting workflow that matches your analysis:

| Your starting point | Recommended workflow | Result |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Dataset and outcome definitions | `cifreport()` | Complete analysis report with tables and figures |
| Fitted `cifcurve()` object | `gtsummary::tbl_survfit()` | Cumulative incidence table |
| Fitted `polyreg()` object | `gtsummary::tbl_regression()` or `modelsummary` | Event-specific effect estimates |

The examples generate and interpret tables and figures. Code using `gtsummary`
requires version 2.6.1 or later; the regression tables also require `broom.helpers`
1.20.0 or later. **Version note (2026-11-16):** `cifreport()` is available in the
GitHub development version of `cifmodeling` but is not exported by CRAN release 1.2.4.
The `cifreport()` examples run only if the function is available. The other
table-formatting examples do not require it. Check your installation with `"cifreport" %in% getNamespaceExports("cifmodeling")`. For an end-to-end analysis, see [Worked
examples](v5_examples.html); for plots, see [Gallery](v6_gallery.html).

```{r reporting-setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
gtsummary_ready <- requireNamespace("gtsummary", quietly = TRUE) &&
  utils::packageVersion("gtsummary") >= "2.6.1"
cifreport_ready <- gtsummary_ready &&
  "cifreport" %in% getNamespaceExports("cifmodeling")
regression_ready <- gtsummary_ready &&
  requireNamespace("broom.helpers", quietly = TRUE) &&
  utils::packageVersion("broom.helpers") >= "1.20.0"
```

## 1. Create a complete report with `cifreport()` {#automated-reports}

`cifreport()` produces baseline characteristics, event counts, estimated
probabilities, unadjusted (crude) risk ratios, curve-comparison tests, and figures. It can
**analyze several outcomes in one report** and export Word, HTML, or PDF files.
The function also returns the tables, plots, fitted models, and analysis status
for inspection in R.

### Create an editable Word report

Supply a dataset, outcome definition, and grouping variable; `cifreport()`
performs the analysis and saves the report. This short example is not executed
during the vignette build because it would write a file:

```{r reporting-save-file, eval=FALSE}
data("diabetes.complications", package = "cifmodeling")
cifreport(
  diabetes.complications,
  outcomes = list(Retinopathy = list(
    time = "t", event = "epsilon", outcome.type = "competing-risk",
    time.point = 8
  )),
  exposure = "fruitq1",
  characteristics = c("age", "sex"),
  filename.cifreport = "diabetes-report.docx"
)
```

Word tables are editable. Use `.html` or `.pdf` filenames for the other
formats, or a vector of filenames to save multiple formats in one analysis.
The directory must already exist; existing files are overwritten. File
output requires Pandoc, Word also needs `xml2` and `zip`, and PDF requires
Chrome, Chromium, or Microsoft Edge (set `CIFREPORT_BROWSER` if necessary).

### Inspect an analysis with two outcomes in R

In `diabetes.complications`, event code 1 denotes diabetic retinopathy, code 2
denotes macrovascular complications, and code 0 denotes censoring. We report
the retinopathy CIF and *complication-free survival*, for which either
complication counts as an event. Follow-up time `t` is measured in years.

```{r reporting-report, eval=cifreport_ready}
library(cifmodeling)
data("diabetes.complications", package = "cifmodeling")

cohort <- transform(diabetes.complications, all_event = epsilon != 0)

report <- cifreport(
  cohort,
  exposure = c("Fruit intake" = "fruitq1"),
  code.exposure.ref = 0,
  characteristics = c("age", "sex"),
  outcomes = list(
    Retinopathy = list(
      time = "t", event = "epsilon", outcome.type = "competing-risk",
      time.point = c(4, 8)
    ),
    "Complication-free survival" = list(
      time = "t", event = "all_event", outcome.type = "survival",
      time.point = c(3, 8)
    )
  ),
  overall = TRUE,
  filename.cifreport = NULL
)

# Estimated probabilities at the requested time points (Table 3)
report$tables$All[["Fruit intake"]]$table3
```

Setting `filename.cifreport = NULL` computes the results **without saving a
file**, allowing you to inspect them before export. The returned
`report$status` data frame records skipped analyses, warnings, and failures. A
failure in one analysis does not necessarily stop the others.

```{r reporting-status, eval=cifreport_ready}
head(report$status)
```

Omit `filename.cifreport` to save a date-stamped Word report in the working
directory. Set it to `NULL` to inspect results without writing a file. You can
specify separate time points and probability scales for each outcome, as in
the example above.

### View results from the report

The table above and figure below are taken directly from the returned
`report` object, not recreated from example numbers. When `cifreport()` is available,
they are generated by the vignette build from the fitted analysis.

```{r reporting-report-figure, eval=cifreport_ready, fig.cap="Retinopathy cumulative incidence figure produced by cifreport()", fig.width=7, fig.height=5, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
report_figure <- report$figures$All[["Fruit intake"]][["Retinopathy"]]
if (is.null(report_figure)) {
  stop("The retinopathy figure was not returned by cifreport().")
}
print(report_figure)
```

To inspect the event counts, probabilities, and analysis status, use
`report$tables` and `report$status`; the example above displays Table 3 and
the first status records. The plot uses the same fitted analysis as the report tables. The Word
export organizes these results into a document with editable tables.

### What does the report contain?

The report includes five tables for each analysis population and exposure definition:

| Table | Contents |
|:--|:--|
| 1 | Baseline patient characteristics, with optional overall column and group-comparison p-values |
| 2 | Observed event and censoring counts over follow-up |
| 3 | Observed cumulative counts and estimated KM or AJ probabilities at the requested times, with pointwise confidence intervals |
| 4 | Unadjusted risk ratios at each requested time, fitted using `polyreg()` |
| 5 | Curve comparison tests: log-rank for survival and Gray for competing risks |

Each figure displays an outcome on the selected probability scale. For a
survival endpoint, the default is KM survival; for competing risks, it is the
primary-event AJ cumulative incidence. Use `estimator = "1-KM"` or
`"1-AJ"` within an outcome definition to report the complementary probability.
Table 4 always concerns **event probabilities**: `1 - KM` for a survival
endpoint and the cause-specific CIFs for competing risks. The reported RRs
are unadjusted; no baseline covariates enter these fits.

### Useful options and scope

Use `subset.condition` to select the analysis population and `subgroup` to
report results separately for each level of a categorical variable. Add multiple
exposures by passing a named vector, for example
`exposure = c("Fruit intake" = "fruitq1", Sex = "sex")`. You can change
exposure reference codes with `code.exposure.ref`, display labels with
`label.strata`, and figure settings with `cifplot.args`. The report's group
labels and order are shared by tables and figures.

```{r reporting-options, eval=FALSE}
cifreport(
  cohort,
  outcomes = list(Retinopathy = list(
    time = "t", event = "epsilon", outcome.type = "competing-risk",
    time.point = 8
  )),
  exposure = "fruitq1",
  subgroup = "sex",
  subset.condition = "age >= 50",
  label.strata = c("0" = "Other intake", "1" = "Low intake"),
  cifplot.args = list(label.x = "Years", add.risktable = FALSE),
  filename.cifreport = NULL
)
```

`cifreport()` supports unweighted, right-censored data with one row per
subject and at most one competing-event code per outcome. It does not fit
adjusted risk-ratio models, handle time-dependent covariates or recurrent
events, or construct simultaneous confidence bands.
Some results may be unavailable: for example, an RR requires adequate
follow-up in each group, and competing-risk regression requires both event
types to have been observed by the requested time. Review `report$status` when preparing
results for publication. For detailed options, see `?cifreport`.

## 2. Report cumulative incidence from `cifcurve()` {#reporting-cumulative-incidence}

If a curve is already fitted, you can create a publication table without
running `cifreport()`. The example uses `gtsummary::tbl_survfit()` on a
reproducible sample of 200 observations from the same diabetes cohort.

### A table of cumulative incidence probabilities

```{r reporting-cif-table, eval=gtsummary_ready}
library(cifmodeling)
library(gtsummary)
data("diabetes.complications", package = "cifmodeling")

set.seed(1)
report_data <- diabetes.complications[
  sample.int(nrow(diabetes.complications), 200L),
]
report_data$fruitq1 <- factor(
  report_data$fruitq1, levels = c(0, 1),
  labels = c("Other intake", "Low intake")
)

curve <- cifcurve(
  Event(t, epsilon) ~ fruitq1, data = report_data,
  outcome.type = "competing-risk"
)

cif_table <- tbl_survfit(
  curve, times = c(4, 8), type = "risk",
  label_header = "**{time}-year CIF**"
)
cif_table
```

For competing risks, `cifcurve()` stores `surv = 1 - CIF` in its
`survfit`-compatible result. Therefore, **`type = "risk"` displays the CIF**,
with the saved confidence limits complemented and reordered as needed.
`tbl_survfit()` uses the fitted estimates and intervals without refitting the
curve.

### Choose the confidence interval before making the table

Specify the variance method, reference distribution, and transformation in
`cifcurve()`, not in `tbl_survfit()`. The next example requests an
influence-function (IF) variance, Student critical values, and a log-log
transformation. On the CIF scale, this corresponds to a complementary log–log
transformation.

```{r reporting-student, eval=gtsummary_ready}
student_curve <- cifcurve(
  Event(t, epsilon) ~ fruitq1, data = report_data,
  outcome.type = "competing-risk",
  error = "if", conf.dist = "t", conf.type = "log-log"
)

student_table <- tbl_survfit(
  student_curve, times = c(4, 8), type = "risk",
  label_header = "**{time}-year CIF**"
) |>
  modify_footnote_header(
    columns = all_stat_cols(),
    footnote = paste(
      "95% pointwise IF-t intervals; log-log transformation of 1 - CIF;",
      "deletion allocation for degrees of freedom."
    )
  )
student_table
```

`error = "fay"` instead requests a Fay–Graubard-type variance correction;
`df.method = "equal"` selects an alternative degrees-of-freedom allocation
for IF-t. All supplied weights are treated as fixed; uncertainty in an
externally estimated propensity score is not included. For the definitions
and limitations, see [Computational formulas](v4_formulas.html).

You can inspect the degrees of freedom and interval status separately,
without adding diagnostic columns to the publication table:

```{r reporting-diagnostics, eval=gtsummary_ready}
s <- summary(student_curve, times = c(4, 8), extend = TRUE)
data.frame(
  group = s$strata, time = s$time,
  df = s$df, interval_status = s$conf.status
)
```

Unavailable intervals remain missing, including beyond observed
positive-weight follow-up. These intervals are **pointwise**, not simultaneous
bands.

### Add a curve-comparison test

The probabilities at 4 and 8 years are fixed-time estimates. By contrast,
`ciftest()` compares curves **over a follow-up period**. The next example
summarizes three tests restricted to eight years of follow-up; it does not
perform a separate test for each column above.

```{r reporting-tests, eval=gtsummary_ready}
tests <- list(
  Gray = ciftest(Event(t, epsilon) ~ fruitq1, report_data,
                 test = "gray", tau = 8),
  Early = ciftest(Event(t, epsilon) ~ fruitq1, report_data,
                  test = "score", rho = 1, gamma = 0, tau = 8),
  Late = ciftest(Event(t, epsilon) ~ fruitq1, report_data,
                 test = "score", rho = 0, gamma = 1, tau = 8)
)

test_results <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(tests), function(name) {
  x <- generics::tidy(tests[[name]])
  data.frame(test = name, statistic = x$statistic, p.value = x$p.value)
}))

as_gtsummary(test_results) |>
  modify_header(
    test = "**Curve comparison through 8 years**",
    statistic = "**Statistic**", p.value = "**p-value**"
  ) |>
  modify_fmt_fun(p.value = label_style_pvalue(digits = 3))
```

The standard Gray test uses its classical covariance estimator; each score test uses
its corresponding variance estimator. For the choice of weights and more advanced
multiple-direction tests, see [Tests of cumulative incidence
functions](v3_gray_extensions.html).

### Export the table

Export the table with standard `gtsummary` converters. Replace the example
filenames with your preferred paths:

```{r reporting-export-cif, eval=FALSE}
gt::gtsave(gtsummary::as_gt(student_table), "cif-table.html")
flextable::save_as_docx(
  gtsummary::as_flex_table(student_table),
  path = "cif-table.docx"
)
```

## 3. Report regression results from `polyreg()` {#reporting-cif-regression}

`polyreg()` estimates effects for both competing events in one joint model.
`gtsummary` can display each event separately or combine their results side by
side. Here, we use the full diabetes cohort, rather than the 200-record sample
above, to estimate **8-year risk ratios** adjusted for age and sex.

### Make an event-specific regression table

```{r reporting-regression, eval=regression_ready}
library(cifmodeling)
library(gtsummary)
data("diabetes.complications", package = "cifmodeling")

regression_data <- diabetes.complications
regression_data$fruitq1 <- factor(
  regression_data$fruitq1, levels = c(0, 1),
  labels = c("Other intake", "Low intake")
)
attr(regression_data$fruitq1, "label") <- "Fruit intake"

fit <- polyreg(
  nuisance.model = Event(t, epsilon) ~ age + sex,
  exposure = "fruitq1", code.exposure.ref = "Other intake",
  data = regression_data, time.point = 8,
  effect.measure1 = "RR", effect.measure2 = "RR"
)

retinopathy_table <- tbl_regression(fit, exponentiate = TRUE)
retinopathy_table
```

By default, the table reports event 1 (diabetic retinopathy). `exponentiate = TRUE`
shows risk ratios and the confidence limits stored in the fit. Standard
errors and test statistics remain on the log-effect scale. These associations
are not automatically causal effects.

### Show both competing events

Set `event = "event2"` to display results for macrovascular complications.
Because the model fits both events jointly, no second fit is needed.

```{r reporting-two-events, eval=regression_ready}
macrovascular_table <- tbl_regression(
  fit, exponentiate = TRUE, event = "event2"
)
tbl_merge(
  list(retinopathy_table, macrovascular_table),
  tab_spanner = c("**Retinopathy**", "**Macrovascular complications**")
)
```

To obtain a tidy data frame of coefficients for both events, use
`generics::tidy(fit, event = "both", exponentiate = TRUE)`.

### Display other effect measures

Select the effect measure **when fitting the model**; formatting the table
does not change it. `polyreg()` supports RR, OR, and SHR. At a fixed time, SHR is a
ratio of cumulative subdistribution hazards, `-log(1 - CIF)`, rather than a
cause-specific hazard ratio. The two events can use different measures.

This example specifies an RR for retinopathy and an SHR for macrovascular
complications:

```{r reporting-mixed-measures, eval=FALSE}
fit_mixed <- polyreg(
  nuisance.model = Event(t, epsilon) ~ age + sex,
  exposure = "fruitq1", code.exposure.ref = "Other intake",
  data = regression_data, time.point = 8,
  effect.measure1 = "RR", effect.measure2 = "SHR"
)
tbl_merge(
  list(tbl_regression(fit_mixed, exponentiate = TRUE),
       tbl_regression(fit_mixed, exponentiate = TRUE, event = "event2")),
  tab_spanner = c("**Retinopathy (RR)**", "**Macrovascular (SHR)**")
)
```

### Confidence intervals and labels

`tbl_regression()` uses the intervals computed by `polyreg()`, including
bootstrap intervals when those are stored. It does not replace them with
ordinary Wald intervals during exponentiation. To specify the fitted confidence
level explicitly, pass `conf.level = fit$conf.int`.

```{r reporting-regression-labels, eval=regression_ready}
tbl_regression(
  fit, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.level = fit$conf.int,
  label = list(fruitq1 ~ "Low fruit intake versus other intake")
)
```

Use `label.exposure` and `label.strata` in `polyreg()` to set display labels
when fitting. For programmatic extraction, `generics::tidy(fit)` returns
log-scale estimates by default; set `exponentiate = TRUE` to obtain ratios.
The usual `tidy()` arguments are logical `conf.int` and numeric `conf.level`.

### Use `modelsummary` or export the regression table

For `modelsummary`, use `as_modelsummary()` to supply event-specific
inference results and display labels. Direct `coef(fit)` and `tidy(fit)` retain the
underlying coefficient names. Set `display.labels = FALSE` in
`as_modelsummary()` if you need those names for `coef_map` or `coef_omit`.

```{r reporting-modelsummary, eval=FALSE}
modelsummary::msummary(
  as_modelsummary(fit, event = "event1"),
  exponentiate = TRUE,
  estimate = "{estimate} [{conf.low}, {conf.high}]",
  statistic = NULL
)
```

Export the `gtsummary` regression table in the same way as the CIF table:

```{r reporting-export-regression, eval=FALSE}
gt::gtsave(gtsummary::as_gt(retinopathy_table), "regression-table.html")
flextable::save_as_docx(
  gtsummary::as_flex_table(retinopathy_table),
  path = "regression-table.docx"
)
```
